messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Mechanic
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells, Stress: Stress, Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mai had never thought of herself as someone who could be frightened. At seventy-six, she had spent more than fifty years working as a mechanic, her hands stained with grease, her back bent over engines that others could not fix. She had raised three children in a small house outside Portland, had buried her mother, had watched her husband retire and then un-retire because he could not sit still. Fear was not something she had made room for. But that was before the man in the white sedan began parking outside her shop.

It started with small things. A coffee cup left on the hood of her car. A note tucked under her windshield wiper that said only her name. Then the calls at night, breathing and nothing else. Mai told herself it was nothing, that the world was full of troubled people, that she was not the kind of woman who needed to be afraid. But her body did not listen. She began to notice smells that should not have been there—damp soil, wet grass, the particular heaviness of air after rain—and each time her stomach turned cold. These smells followed her: in the alley behind the shop, in her own garden when she tried to water the tomatoes, even once in her kitchen when her husband came in from mowing the lawn. She could not explain why they frightened her. She only knew that they did.

The memory of the worst night came to her in fragments that refused to form a whole story. She remembered the photograph perfectly—a single image, frozen and clear, as if someone had pressed pause on a movie. It was the man’s face, inches from her car window, his expression flat and unreadable, the streetlight catching the sweat on his forehead. She could see that photograph in her mind at any moment, sharp and complete. But when she tried to tell her daughter what had happened next, the words collapsed. She would start, and then the thread would vanish, and she would find herself staring at the wall, unable to finish a single sentence. She had learned to stop trying. She pushed the memory away before it could fully arrive, like slamming a door on someone’s fingers.

Over the months that followed, Mai’s world shrank. She stopped walking to the corner store. She stopped sitting in her backyard. She became watchful in a way that exhausted her—scanning every parking lot, every rearview mirror, every shadow that moved at the edge of her vision. She looked behind her constantly, a quick turn of the head that her husband called a nervous habit but that she knew was a necessity. Even inside her own home, she could not let her guard down. She locked doors she had never locked before. She checked the locks twice. She sat with her back to the wall during dinner, though she did not tell her husband why.

The worst part, the part she could not admit to anyone, was that happiness had become dangerous. When she felt relaxed—when a customer smiled at her work, when her granddaughter laughed on the phone—a spike of fear would pierce the moment. She had come to believe that feeling good was a trap, that the moment she let her guard down, something terrible would find her again. So she stayed tense. It felt safer.

Her work suffered. She had always been fast, but now she double-checked every bolt, every seal, and still she found herself losing focus when a customer walked in unexpectedly. Her boss said nothing, but she saw him watching her. She had always been the one everyone relied on. Now she felt like a woman holding a cup of water that was about to spill.

What finally brought her to a clinic was a single afternoon in late October. She had been standing under a customer’s car, tightening an oil pan, when she smelled soil—fresh, damp, unmistakable. Her hands went numb. She dropped the wrench. She lay on the concrete floor, staring up at the undercarriage, unable to move, until her coworker found her and helped her sit up. That night, her husband held her hand and told her she needed to talk to someone. She did not argue. She was tired of being afraid of the smell of earth. She was tired of being afraid of her own relief. She wanted to tell the story from beginning to end, without losing the thread, without slamming the door. She wanted to finish a sentence about that night and let it be over.
